extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers (especially short-story and memoir writers), creative-writing students and teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance on writing short stories, novels, and memoirs: how to handle moral ambiguity, reader engagement, truthfulness in memoir, shaping memory into narrative, and the role of teaching and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral ambiguity and character decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters face moral decisions and the tension in a story often comes from watching how a character will act; the sum of decisions is who we are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not set out to 'create a moral.' Focus on the process by which people create themselves through choices. Present consequences of decisions rather than issuing judgments; avoid overt moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sermonizing / no 'thumb on the scales'
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction that feels like a sermon or has a visible 'thumb on the scales' weakens engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer writing that explores rather than proclaims. If the story is instructive rather than inquisitive, readers may be turned off; let moral complexity emerge from action and character, not authorial preaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art of implication in the short story
rubrics_metrics.description: The short story is an art of implication: you don't tell everything; you test the reader's willingness and invite participation in deciphering a life from the moments shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on suggestion and omission to engage readers; accept that many readers prefer more explicit closure, but the short story's power is often in what it leaves unsaid. Use tight, focused moments rather than full chronological arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form fit: different demands and pleasures of novel vs short story
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels allow a reader to 'live in the world' of the book over time and to return to characters day after day; short stories demand an intense, immediate engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose form according to the reader experience you want to create. Expect different structural and pacing choices for novels (breadth, unfolding over time) versus short stories (concentration, immediacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing inner complexity rather than simplistic motives
rubrics_metrics.description: People's motives are often obscure even to themselves; giving readers access to a character's thoughts and emotions complicates outsider judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray the disjunction between appearance and reality. Use interiority to reveal ambiguity and conflicted motives rather than reducing characters to simple self-interest or archetypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaping memory into narrative (narrative selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning memories or experiences into stories imposes a shape on things that did not originally have shape; context (faces, weather, body language) matters and memory is selective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that narrative choices inevitably alter events; acknowledge the constructedness of recollection while striving for truthful representation of what memory yields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and vulnerability in memoir
rubrics_metrics.description: The memoirist should be committed to telling the truth that their memory tells them without evasion, dodging, or prettifying; best memoirs often show the author's complicity and shortcomings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let yourself be seen as you really are, even less heroic. Avoid protecting or prettifying your portrayal; include complicity and difficult material rather than eliding it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intention governs the 'honor' of memoir
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral standing of a memoir largely depends on the writer's intention: whether they are committed to truthful representation or are seeking to protect/beautify themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intention matters. Memoirs written to secure an attractive self-portrait are suspect; strive for sincerity and willingness to be critical of oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations and sensitivity when work is factual
rubrics_metrics.description: Books adapted into other media require changes; adaptations of memoirs can feel like violations because they involve real people and events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and accept that film/theater adaptations will alter material for drama, but be aware of the ethical and emotional stakes when the source is factual. Differentiate emotional reactions between adapting fiction and memoir.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching's role: cultivate self-editing and awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers can help writers become better editors of their own work and make them more aware of what they are and are not doing; they can introduce useful reading models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the classroom to develop students' critical self-awareness and editorial judgment, recommend writers whose gifts complement students' strengths, and encourage adventurousness. Teaching cannot implant raw talent but can refine practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of paralyzing self-consciousness from over-instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly talking about strategies, endings, beginnings, tone and style can make a writer obsessively self-conscious and paralyzed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance craft discussion with sustained writing practice. Avoid letting analytical description of craft substitute for the act of writing; be cautious that instruction does not inhibit creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and peer feedback as central learning tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement comes from doing the work repeatedly and having a group of passionate, canny readers to provide feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage frequent practice and workshop-style feedback. A 'captive audience' of engaged readers helps authors see what they're doing and can accelerate development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability/truthfulness applies to fiction as well as memoir
rubrics_metrics.description: There are dishonest fictions as well as dishonest memoirs; dishonest fiction is that which is not written from a point of vulnerability or truthfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write fiction from a place of emotional honesty; avoid evasive or propagandistic storytelling even when the work is invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation and voice: complexity when characters 'borrow' stories
rubrics_metrics.description: A character's appropriation of another's story (presenting it as confession) can be a means of self-discovery and entrapment, complicating simple moral judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriation as a device to reveal character psychology and the murky lines between discovery, ownership, and self-representation; show internal consequences rather than treating it as mere theft.
